title: What is the Java compilation and execution flow — `.java` source → `javac` compiler → `.class` bytecode → JVM class loading → bytecode verification → interpretation + JIT compilation → native execution — and what is the classpath (where the JVM/compiler look for `.class` files and JARs)?
shortTitle: What is the Java compilation and execution flow?

s1_definition.profdef: Java source code in a `.java` file is compiled by `javac` into platform-neutral `.class` bytecode. At runtime the JVM loads each class through a class loader, verifies the bytecode for safety, links and initializes the class, then begins executing. Execution starts in the interpreter, and the Just-In-Time compiler progressively compiles frequently executed methods into native machine code for speed. The classpath is the ordered list of directories and JAR files where both the compiler and the JVM search for `.class` files and dependencies.
s1_definition.analogy: Writing Java is like filling out a transfer form in your own handwriting (the `.java` source). The `javac` compiler is the clerk who re-types it onto the bank's standard internal form that any branch understands (the `.class` bytecode). The JVM is the branch that receives the standard form, checks it is genuine and complete (verification), and starts processing it carefully by hand (interpretation). When it sees you make the same transfer every month, it sets up a fast standing instruction so future runs are instant (JIT to native code). The classpath is simply the list of filing cabinets the branch searches to find the forms and reference documents it needs.
s1_definition.oneliner: `javac` turns source into portable bytecode, the JVM loads, verifies, interprets and JIT-compiles it to native code, and the classpath tells both tools where to find classes and JARs.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Java source code in a `.java` file is compiled by `javac` into platform-neutral `.class` bytecode. At runtime the JVM loads each class through a class loader, verifies the bytecode for safety, links and initializes the class, then begins executing. Execution starts in the interpreter, and the Just-In-Time compiler progressively compiles frequently executed methods into native machine code for speed. The classpath is the ordered list of directories and JAR files where both the compiler and the JVM search for `.class` files and dependencies.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Writing Java is like filling out a transfer form in your own handwriting (the `.java` source). The `javac` compiler is the clerk who re-types it onto the bank's standard internal form that any branch understands (the `.class` bytecode). The JVM is the branch that receives the standard form, checks it is genuine and complete (verification), and starts processing it carefully by hand (interpretation). When it sees you make the same transfer every month, it sets up a fast standing instruction so future runs are instant (JIT to native code). The classpath is simply the list of filing cabinets the branch searches to find the forms and reference documents it needs.

**One line to remember:** `javac` turns source into portable bytecode, the JVM loads, verifies, interprets and JIT-compiles it to native code, and the classpath tells both tools where to find classes and JARs.

sections.s2_technical:
The journey begins with a `.java` file containing source code. You invoke the compiler, for example `javac -d out TransferService.java`, and `javac` checks the syntax, resolves types, enforces the language rules, and emits one `.class` file per class or nested type. That `.class` file contains bytecode, which is a compact instruction set for an abstract stack machine, not instructions for any real CPU. This indirection is exactly why Java is portable: the same `.class` file runs on Windows, Linux, and macOS because each platform ships its own JVM.

When you run `java com.bank.TransferService`, the JVM must first find and load that class. Loading is done by class loaders arranged in a parent-first hierarchy: the bootstrap loader handles core JDK classes, the platform loader handles standard modules, and the application loader handles your classes found on the classpath. A loader reads the `.class` bytes and produces a `Class` object in memory. You can observe this at runtime: `TransferService.class.getClassLoader()` returns the application class loader for your own classes and null for core classes like `String` loaded by the bootstrap loader.

After loading comes verification, a security step where the JVM proves the bytecode is well-formed: the operand stack never underflows or overflows, types are consistent, and no instruction jumps to an illegal location. This is why a corrupted or hand-crafted malicious class is rejected before it can run. Verification is followed by preparation, where static fields get default values, and resolution, where symbolic references to other classes are turned into direct references. Finally initialization runs the static initializers and static field assignments; this is the moment a static block executes.

Once a method is ready, execution starts in the interpreter, which walks the bytecode one instruction at a time. This starts fast to warm up but is slow for hot loops. The JVM's profiler counts how often methods and loops run, and when a method crosses a threshold the Just-In-Time compiler compiles it to native machine code tuned for the actual CPU, applying optimizations like inlining and escape analysis. HotSpot uses tiered compilation, moving from the quick C1 compiler to the aggressive C2 compiler as a method proves itself hot, which is why a long-running banking service gets faster in its first minutes and then stays fast.

The classpath ties it all together. It is an ordered list of entries, each either a directory holding a package tree of `.class` files or a JAR archive. The compiler searches it to resolve types you reference, and the JVM searches it to load classes at runtime. You set it with the `-cp` flag, for example `java -cp "out:libs/*" com.bank.TransferService`, where the first entry is your compiled output and `libs/*` expands to every JAR in that folder. Order matters because the first matching class on the path wins, which is the usual cause of a confusing wrong-version bug when two JARs contain the same class. A senior-level nuance is that the modern module path is a stricter alternative to the classpath that enforces explicit dependencies and strong encapsulation, but the classpath remains the default for most applications.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India our customers are Rajesh, a software engineer with savings account SAV2001 holding ten lakh rupees, and Priya, a property owner with current account CUR3001 holding two lakh fifty thousand rupees.

Problem 1 — a new developer runs our transfer program and gets a confusing "could not find or load main class" error even though the code compiled fine. The real cause is almost always the classpath: the JVM is looking in the wrong folder for the `.class` file. We want a demo that makes the compile-then-run flow explicit so the team sees exactly where bytecode lands and how the classpath points at it.

Problem 2 — the operations team notices our settlement batch is slow for the first thirty seconds after a restart and then speeds up, and they suspect a bug. It is not a bug; it is the JVM interpreting first and then JIT-compiling the hot transfer loop into native code. We want to demonstrate that warm-up by running the same transfer thousands of times and observing it get cheaper per iteration.

Our runnable demo will define an `Account` class with debit and credit, a `TransferService` with a `transfer` method, and a `main` that first does one clear transfer from Rajesh to Priya to illustrate ordinary execution, then runs a large loop of tiny transfers to let the JIT warm up, printing timing for the first batch versus a later batch so the interpreter-to-native transition is visible. The bash section will show the full `javac` then `java` flow and an explicit classpath.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# STEP 1 — compile: .java source becomes .class bytecode in the out/ directory
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/flow/*.java

# STEP 2 — inspect the generated bytecode (optional but instructive)
javap -c out/com/bank/flow/TransferService.class

# STEP 3 — run: -cp points the classpath at out/; JVM loads, verifies, JITs
java -cp out com.bank.flow.CompilationFlowDemo

# Classpath with extra JARs: order matters, first match wins
java -cp "out:libs/*" com.bank.flow.CompilationFlowDemo

# See JIT compilation happen (prints each method as it is compiled to native)
java -XX:+PrintCompilation -cp out com.bank.flow.CompilationFlowDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the source file `CompilationFlowDemo.java` plus its sibling classes, Rajesh (SAV2001, 1000000), Priya (CUR3001, 250000), and a rent amount of 50000.

Step 1 — `javac -d out` reads each `.java` file, checks the language rules, and writes one `.class` file per class into `out/com/bank/flow/`. The data is now portable bytecode, identical on every operating system.

Step 2 — `java -cp out ...` starts the JVM. The application class loader searches the classpath entry `out`, finds `CompilationFlowDemo.class`, reads the bytes, and creates the in-memory `Class` object. Classes it references, like `Account` and `TransferService`, are loaded lazily the first time they are needed.

Step 3 — the JVM verifies the bytecode for safety, prepares static fields, resolves references, and then initializes the class, which runs the static block. That is why the logger is configured before `main` executes.

Step 4 — `main` runs in the interpreter. The single transfer debits Rajesh by 50000, taking him from 1000000 to 950000, and credits Priya by 50000, taking her from 250000 to 300000.

Step 5 — the cold loop runs 200,000 tiny transfers. Early iterations are interpreted and the profiler counts the hot `transfer`, `debit`, and `credit` methods. Partway through, the JIT compiles them to native code.

Step 6 — the hot loop runs another 200,000 transfers, now executing the already-native-compiled methods, so it completes measurably faster than the cold loop, demonstrating the interpreter-to-JIT transition. The total transfer count reaches 400,000.

Final output:

```text
2026-10-30 19:21:10 INFO    Loaded by: jdk.internal.loader.ClassLoaders$AppClassLoader@...
2026-10-30 19:21:10 INFO    After single transfer -> Rajesh=950000 Priya=300000
2026-10-30 19:21:10 INFO    Cold batch (interpreter + early JIT) took 42 ms
2026-10-30 19:21:10 INFO    Hot batch (JIT-compiled to native) took 11 ms
2026-10-30 19:21:10 INFO    Total transfers executed: 400000
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  CompilationFlowDemo.java (source)
    │ javac -d out
    ▼
  out/com/bank/flow/*.class (portable bytecode)
    │ java -cp out  (classpath entry = out)
    ▼
  JVM Class Loader (bootstrap → platform → application)
    │ reads bytes → Class object
    ▼
  Bytecode Verification (stack, types, jumps all valid)
    │
    ▼
  Prepare → Resolve → Initialize (static block runs, logger configured)
    │
    ▼
  Interpreter executes main()
    │ single transfer: Rajesh 1,000,000 → 950,000 ; Priya 250,000 → 300,000
    │ hot loop detected by profiler
    ▼
  JIT Compiler (C1 → C2) → native machine code
    │ hot batch runs ~4x faster than cold batch
    ▼
  Native CPU execution → result logged
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Java execution model has a clean, well-defined pipeline that I like to walk through end to end. It starts with source code in a dot java file. The javac compiler reads that source, enforces the language rules, and produces dot class files containing bytecode, which is a portable instruction set for an abstract machine rather than for any real processor. That single indirection is the reason the same compiled class runs unchanged on Windows, Linux, and macOS, because every platform ships its own Java Virtual Machine that understands the common bytecode.

At runtime the JVM loads the class through a parent-first hierarchy of class loaders, where the bootstrap loader handles core library classes and the application loader handles our own classes found on the classpath. Immediately after loading the JVM verifies the bytecode to prove it is safe, checking that the operand stack is consistent, the types line up, and no instruction jumps somewhere illegal, which is what protects us from corrupted or malicious classes. Then it prepares and resolves references and runs class initialization, which is the moment static blocks execute.

Execution itself begins in the interpreter, which walks the bytecode one instruction at a time so startup is quick. Meanwhile a profiler counts how often each method runs, and when a method becomes hot the Just-In-Time compiler compiles it to native machine code tuned to the actual CPU, applying optimizations like inlining. HotSpot does this in tiers, moving from a fast compiler to a more aggressive one, which is exactly why a long-running service speeds up in its first minutes and then stays fast.

The classpath is what both the compiler and the JVM use to find classes. It is an ordered list of directories and JAR files, set with the minus cp flag, and order matters because the first matching class wins, which is the usual explanation when someone loads the wrong version of a library.

In our platform at National Bank of India this understanding mattered in practice. The operations team once reported that our settlement batch was slow for the first thirty seconds after every restart and then sped up, and they thought it was a bug. I explained it was the JVM interpreting the hot transfer loop first and then JIT-compiling it into native code, and I proved it by running the same transfer loop twice and showing the second batch finishing several times faster. On another occasion a new developer hit a could-not-find-main-class error even though compilation succeeded, and the fix was simply pointing the classpath at the correct output directory, which is the single most common classpath mistake I have seen.

---

keyPoints: java command starts JVM, which loads .class files
Classpath tells JVM where to find .class files and JARs
-cp or -classpath flag, or CLASSPATH environment variable
Module path (Java 9+): --module-path replaces classpath for modules
